sections.h2: What the planner does, step by step
p: Step one adds up the appliances you tick: the watts that run at once and the units they use in a day. Step two sizes the inverter for that running load with a safety margin, and step four can raise it so the inverter accepts the solar array. Step three sizes the battery for only the load you want to keep on during loadshedding, for the hours you choose. Step four sizes the solar array for your daily units and your city's sun. Step five splits a month's solar between what you use while the sun is up and what you export, and compares the bill with and without net billing: the energy charge alone, and the whole bill with fixed charge, surcharges and GST. Step six sizes a generator for the whole list, in case you want one for long outages.

Step seven is the decision. It prices four setups with the dated price data behind the solar price and backup cost calculators: on-grid solar (the array above, installed), hybrid solar (the same array with the battery bank and a hybrid inverter), a UPS or petrol generator for the backup load only, and on-grid solar together with that UPS or generator. Each gets a price range, the backup it gives, the monthly bill saving or running cost, and the net cost over the years you pick: price plus battery replacements plus running cost minus bill saving. The cheapest net setup that gives your backup hours is recommended; with a budget, a setup counts when the low end of its price range fits it (leave the budget blank for no limit). When the runner-up's range of net cost overlaps the pick's, the result says it is a close call, so get quotes for both. On-grid solar earns only while the grid is on: the planner spreads your power cut hours evenly over the day, so a hybrid also exports only while the grid is on, and a generator is credited with the grid units it supplies.

What this comparison leaves out: installation of the UPS or generator (their prices are equipment only), battery losses on solar self-use, inverter replacement, the daytime solar the hybrid battery stores, the leftover value of a battery replaced near the end of the period, and price changes over the years (every figure is in today's rupees). Power cuts are spread evenly over the day, so cuts that fall mostly at midday cost on-grid solar more than shown. To compare backup costs in detail, the UPS vs solar vs generator calculator prices the same backup on equipment and running cost alone and leaves out the bill saving, so its cheapest pick can differ from the one here. To size a generator for motors and the rest of your own list, with each starting surge shown, use the generator size calculator.
Every step is a calculator on this site. Open any of them from the task cards below to change its assumptions, see worked examples and read the formula.

Start with the task, not the jargon. If the lights go out during loadshedding, start with the battery and UPS tools. If the bill is the problem, start with the bill calculators and the AC consumption tool. If you are planning solar, add up your home load first, then size the system.

Each result page ends with a Next step link to the tool that naturally follows, so a battery backup time leads to inverter sizing, a home load leads to solar sizing, and a wire size leads to the breaker to pair with it.

sections.h2: Why the numbers can be trusted
p: The calculators share one engine with one set of formulas and one set of constants. The same formula produces the live result, the worked examples, the reference tables and the FAQ answers on every page, so every number comes from one engine; where two pages show a different bill for the same units, each one names its own inputs, such as the sanctioned load and the FPA.

The formulas follow standard electrical practice (IEC and NEPRA performance standards for a 230 V, 400 V three-phase, fifty hertz supply). Assumptions that depend on judgement are marked and editable, and a review by a PEC-registered electrical engineer is in progress.

faq.q: Can I save or share my plan?
faq.a: Yes. Press the plan button, then use Save as PDF to print or keep the page, WhatsApp to send the sizes and a link to your installer, or copy the link: it carries your appliance list, so whoever opens it sees the same plan.

faq.q: Which is better for my home: solar, hybrid solar or a UPS?
faq.a: It depends on the backup you need, your bill and your budget, so the planner compares four setups for your own list. For the example home, on-grid solar costs Rs 363,750 to Rs 602,000 and saves Rs 12,189 a month (only while the grid is on) but gives no backup, because an on-grid inverter switches off in a power cut. Hybrid solar adds 1 lithium pack of 5.12 kWh (51.2 V) and a grid-tie hybrid inverter that can still export, and costs Rs 578,750 to Rs 912,000 (the hybrid inverter's extra cost over an on-grid one is added only where our price lists show one; the result says which). A UPS 1.2 kVA + 2 tubular batteries costs Rs 115,239 to Rs 191,500 and costs about Rs 1,162 a month to run (a UPS through the bill, a generator in petrol and oil, though a generator also takes the backup units it supplies off the bill). On-grid solar with that UPS 1.2 kVA + 2 tubular batteries costs Rs 478,989 to Rs 793,500 and gives backup and most of the bill saving (a UPS recharge comes off it). Over 10 years the recommended setup is Hybrid solar 3.51 kW + 1 lithium pack of 5.12 kWh (51.2 V). Prices are ranges from dated data and the middle price decides, with a close call flagged when the ranges overlap; solar prices include installation, UPS and generator prices are equipment only, and a battery replaced near the end of the period is counted in full.

faq.q: How does the planner work out the saving on the whole bill?
faq.a: It prices 402 units the way the bill calculator does: energy charge, fixed charge for your sanctioned load, FC surcharge and GST, for Rs 22,361. With solar you import 201 units, billed the same way at Rs 10,266, and the 226 exported units earn Rs 1,834, set against that bill, leaving Rs 8,432. The whole-bill saving is Rs 13,929, of which Rs 10,836 is energy charge; the rest is the lower fixed charge band, surcharge and GST. QTA and FPA change month to month and are left at zero here, and the planner assumes GST is charged on the imported units before the export credit, the cautious reading. The buyback rate is NEPRA's national average energy purchase price for CY 2026; it stays editable because NEPRA sets it again each year. Agreements signed before 9 February 2026 stay on the old net-metering terms until they expire, unless the system is enlarged, which moves it to net billing.
Yes. Every tool runs in your browser, needs no sign-up and stores nothing about you. You can share a result by copying the page link after you press Calculate.

faq.q: Do the tools work outside Pakistan?
faq.a: Yes. The defaults are set for Pakistan (230 V single phase, rupees, local tariff slabs), and the converters, battery, solar and wiring tools let you switch to 120 V or enter your own voltage and prices.

They are planning estimates built on typical values. Real backup time, bills and solar output depend on battery age, weather, the exact appliance and the tariff of the month, so expect the real number to land near the estimate, not exactly on it.

faq.q: Who writes and checks the tools?
faq.a: Wattlyst is written by its founder, Ali Ahmad, with formulas documented on the methodology page. Technical review by a PEC-registered electrical engineer is in progress and will be named on each page once complete.

key_facts: The planner carries one appliance list through the whole chain: running load, inverter, battery, solar, net billing and generator, each with the formula of its own calculator, so the sizes never contradict each other.

The decision step compares on-grid solar, hybrid solar with a battery, a UPS or petrol generator, and on-grid solar with that UPS or generator, for the same home: price range, backup time, bill saving and running cost a month, and the net cost over the years you choose. It recommends the setup with the lowest net cost that gives the backup you asked for and fits your budget.

Inverter size = running watts × 1.25, raised if needed so the solar array is at most 1.3 times it; battery Ah = backup watts × hours ÷ (bank volts × usable depth of discharge × inverter efficiency); solar kW = daily units ÷ city yield (the grid covers the moments when everything runs at once), with net billing counting, and the setups pricing, the array only up to the sanctioned load; generator kVA = the larger of running × 1.25 and the starting peak, ÷ 0.8.
Default values (inverter efficiency 85% UPS and 90% hybrid, usable battery capacity 50% tubular and 90% lithium, power factor 0.8) are listed on the methodology page and editable in each calculator.

Pakistan tariff slabs, peak sun hours by city and appliance wattages live in dated data files; the net-billing buyback rate is NEPRA's national average energy purchase price for CY 2026 under the NEPRA (Prosumer) Regulations 2026, notified 9 Feb 2026, and stays editable.
Results are planning estimates, not an official bill or an engineer's design; wiring and solar work must be confirmed by a licensed electrician.

how.text: Your list runs 2,085 W at once (2,535 W when the biggest motor starts) and uses 13.2 units a day, 402 a month. Battery: 500 W × 4 h = 2 kWh ÷ (24 V × 90% usable × 90% inverter) = 103 Ah. Solar: energy 13.2 kWh ÷ 4 kWh per kW per day = 3.31 kW; with the grid connected the array is sized by energy, because the grid supplies the rest whenever the 2,085 W running load is more than the panels give, so 3.31 kW needs 6 panels of 585 W = 3.51 kW making about 427 units a month. Inverter: the larger of 2,085 W × 1.25 = 2.61 kW and the 3.51 kW solar array ÷ 1.3 = 2.7 kW (an inverter takes panels up to about 1.3 times its rating, so it must be at least the array divided by that), so 2.7 kW. Net billing counts an array up to your 4 kW sanctioned load: 6 panels, 3.51 kW, about 427 units a month; the setups below are priced at this array. You use 201 of those units yourself, export 226 at Rs 8.13 and import 201; energy charge Rs 15,652 before solar, Rs 4,816 after, saving Rs 10,836 a month on the energy charge alone. Whole bill (fixed charge, FC surcharge, GST 18%): Rs 22,361 before, Rs 10,266 for the imported units, less Rs 1,834 export credit, leaves Rs 8,432 to pay (Rs 0 credit carried to next month), saving Rs 13,929 a month. Generator for the whole list: 3.3 kVA, next standard size 3.5 kVA. Decision over 10 years, net = price + battery replacements + every month of those years × (running cost − bill saving), in today's rupees. Power cuts take 4 hours a day, spread evenly over the day, so on-grid solar works 83.3% of the time and a hybrid exports only then; a generator's petrol is set against the grid units it supplies. On-grid solar 3.51 kW, installed: Rs 363,750 to Rs 602,000, saves Rs 12,189 a month (only while the grid is on), no backup in a cut, net Rs 979,769 saved. Hybrid solar 3.51 kW + 1 lithium pack of 5.12 kWh (51.2 V): Rs 578,750 to Rs 912,000 (the on-grid price plus Rs 262,500 of battery; extra cost not known (none added) for a 2.7 kW grid-tie hybrid inverter), saves Rs 13,624 a month (exports only while the grid is on), battery replacements Rs 262,500, net Rs 626,969 saved. UPS 1.2 kVA + 2 tubular batteries for 500 W: Rs 115,239 to Rs 191,500, grid recharge adds Rs 1,162 a month to the bill, net Rs 632,170 cost. On-grid solar 3.51 kW + UPS 1.2 kVA + 2 tubular batteries: Rs 478,989 to Rs 793,500, saves Rs 11,187 a month with the recharge on the bill, net Rs 366,800 saved. Recommended, the lowest net that gives your backup: Hybrid solar 3.51 kW + 1 lithium pack of 5.12 kWh (51.2 V). Close call: On-grid solar 3.51 kW + UPS 1.2 kVA + 2 tubular batteries is within the price ranges, so get quotes for both.

Poori list ke liye generator: 3.3 kVA, agla standard size 3.5 kVA. 10 saal ka faisla, kul = qeemat + battery badalna + un saalon ka har mahina × (kharcha − bill ki bachat), aaj ke rupay mein. Bijli 4 ghante band rehti hai, din bhar barabar baant kar, is liye on-grid solar 83.3% waqt chalta hai aur hybrid sirf tab export karta hai; generator ke petrol mein se woh grid units minha hote hain jo woh deta hai. On-grid solar 3.51 kW, installed: Rs 363,750 to Rs 602,000, saves Rs 12,189 a month (only while the grid is on), no backup in a cut, net Rs 979,769 saved. Hybrid solar 3.51 kW + 1 lithium pack of 5.12 kWh (51.2 V): Rs 578,750 to Rs 912,000 (the on-grid price plus Rs 262,500 of battery; extra cost not known (none added) for a 2.7 kW grid-tie hybrid inverter), saves Rs 13,624 a month (exports only while the grid is on), battery replacements Rs 262,500, net Rs 626,969 saved. UPS 1.2 kVA + 2 tubular batteries for 500 W: Rs 115,239 to Rs 191,500, grid recharge adds Rs 1,162 a month to the bill, net Rs 632,170 cost. On-grid solar 3.51 kW + UPS 1.2 kVA + 2 tubular batteries: Rs 478,989 to Rs 793,500, saves Rs 11,187 a month with the recharge on the bill, net Rs 366,800 saved. Recommended, the lowest net that gives your backup: Hybrid solar 3.51 kW + 1 lithium pack of 5.12 kWh (51.2 V). Close call: On-grid solar 3.51 kW + UPS 1.2 kVA + 2 tubular batteries is within the price ranges, so get quotes for both.

mainEntity.name: Can I save or share my plan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Press the plan button, then use Save as PDF to print or keep the page, WhatsApp to send the sizes and a link to your installer, or copy the link: it carries your appliance list, so whoever opens it sees the same plan.

mainEntity.name: Which is better for my home: solar, hybrid solar or a UPS?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the backup you need, your bill and your budget, so the planner compares four setups for your own list. For the example home, on-grid solar costs Rs 363,750 to Rs 602,000 and saves Rs 12,189 a month (only while the grid is on) but gives no backup, because an on-grid inverter switches off in a power cut. Hybrid solar adds 1 lithium pack of 5.12 kWh (51.2 V) and a grid-tie hybrid inverter that can still export, and costs Rs 578,750 to Rs 912,000 (the hybrid inverter's extra cost over an on-grid one is added only where our price lists show one; the result says which). A UPS 1.2 kVA + 2 tubular batteries costs Rs 115,239 to Rs 191,500 and costs about Rs 1,162 a month to run (a UPS through the bill, a generator in petrol and oil, though a generator also takes the backup units it supplies off the bill). On-grid solar with that UPS 1.2 kVA + 2 tubular batteries costs Rs 478,989 to Rs 793,500 and gives backup and most of the bill saving (a UPS recharge comes off it). Over 10 years the recommended setup is Hybrid solar 3.51 kW + 1 lithium pack of 5.12 kWh (51.2 V). Prices are ranges from dated data and the middle price decides, with a close call flagged when the ranges overlap; solar prices include installation, UPS and generator prices are equipment only, and a battery replaced near the end of the period is counted in full.

mainEntity.name: How does the planner work out the saving on the whole bill?

acceptedAnswer.text: It prices 402 units the way the bill calculator does: energy charge, fixed charge for your sanctioned load, FC surcharge and GST, for Rs 22,361. With solar you import 201 units, billed the same way at Rs 10,266, and the 226 exported units earn Rs 1,834, set against that bill, leaving Rs 8,432. The whole-bill saving is Rs 13,929, of which Rs 10,836 is energy charge; the rest is the lower fixed charge band, surcharge and GST. QTA and FPA change month to month and are left at zero here, and the planner assumes GST is charged on the imported units before the export credit, the cautious reading. The buyback rate is NEPRA's national average energy purchase price for CY 2026; it stays editable because NEPRA sets it again each year. Agreements signed before 9 February 2026 stay on the old net-metering terms until they expire, unless the system is enlarged, which moves it to net billing.

mainEntity.name: Do the tools work outside Pakistan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The defaults are set for Pakistan (230 V single phase, rupees, local tariff slabs), and the converters, battery, solar and wiring tools let you switch to 120 V or enter your own voltage and prices.

They are planning estimates built on typical values. Real backup time, bills and solar output depend on battery age, weather, the exact appliance and the tariff of the month, so expect the real number to land near the estimate, not exactly on it.

mainEntity.name: Who writes and checks the tools?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wattlyst is written by its founder, Ali Ahmad, with formulas documented on the methodology page. Technical review by a PEC-registered electrical engineer is in progress and will be named on each page once complete.
